USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the Beijing talks that are opening now to test whether China will move on forced tech transfer, IP theft, and industrial subsidies, while leaving the proposed Section 301 list and the ZTE denial order in place as leverage. Do not impose the $50B tariffs this week, do not broaden them, and do not trade ZTE relief or a tariff pause for a purchase-only package. Instruct the Mnuchin–Lighthizer–Ross team to keep talking if Beijing only offers deficit cosmetics; accept no new U.S. commitments until structural terms are on paper.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: For the United States this is still a leverage window, not an existential threat. The 301 report (2018-03-22) documented unreasonable IP/tech-transfer practices; the proposed ~$50B list (2018-04-03) and the 16 April ZTE component ban have put Chinese high-tech and a major national champion at risk before any U.S. tariff has actually landed. U.S. macro is not yet paying a trade-war tax: Michigan sentiment is 98, industrial production is up, VIX has settled near 16 after the February spike, and the goods deficit has not blown out. China’s already-in-force $3B 232 retaliation (2018-04-02) and its proposed $50B list aimed at soybeans, autos, and aircraft (2018-04-04) are real—ASA called soy tariffs “devastating” and China took ~$12B of U.S. soy last year—so the score is not a clean opportunity. That is why threat sits at −0.30 rather than −0.50: farm-belt and aircraft exposure plus split U.S. objectives (deficit cut vs structural reform) are genuine costs, but they are still prospective. Action stays at 0 / negotiate because talks with Liu He begin this week, Lighthizer and Ross have already downplayed a breakthrough, a Chinese official said MIC 2025 is non-negotiable, and experts expect at best an agreement to keep talking plus a short-term purchase offer. Escalating tariffs or another entity-list strike during the first serious negotiation would waste ZTE leverage, hand Beijing a multilateral narrative, and invite the soy/auto list to go live. Conceding purchases or rolling back 301/ZTE before structural movement would cash in the only tools that produced this meeting.
key_factors: Section 301 list (~$50B) is proposed, not in force; comment period still open through mid-May
ZTE seven-year denial order is live and gives the U.S. precise tech leverage
China has already hit ~$3B of U.S. goods and proposed matching $50B tariffs on soy, autos, and aircraft
Beijing talks with Liu He are starting now; breakthrough on MIC 2025/IP is widely seen as unlikely
U.S. real economy still healthy (sentiment, IP, calmed VIX); dispute not yet a GDP event
U.S. goods exports to China are softer in the window; farm-belt political exposure is the main U.S. vulnerability

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR Section 301 report finds China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable; Trump directs tariffs, a WTO case, and investment restrictions.
USTR publishes proposed Section 301 list: ~1,300 Chinese lines (~$50B) targeting aerospace, ICT, robotics, machinery. Public comment opens.
China announces proposed retaliatory tariffs on ~$50B of US goods including soybeans, automobiles, and aircraft.
US Commerce bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
China imposes retaliatory tariffs on about $3B of US goods (pork, fruit, nuts, wine) in response to Section 232.
U.S. consumer sentiment still high at 98 (May 2018) after a 101.4 March peak—no collapse in household confidence.
VIX back near 16 on 2018-05-02 after the February spike into the 30s; markets are not pricing a crisis.
U.S. industrial production firmer into spring 2018; the tariff fight is not yet visible as an output shock.
U.S. goods exports to China softer in the lookback window (latest ~$10.4B vs ~$13.6B in Dec 2017), a vulnerability if soy/auto tariffs go live.

Mnuchin–Liu He talks launching; breakthrough on structural policy seen highly unlikely; China may offer purchases/opening; official says MIC 2025 is not negotiable; Lighthizer and Ross downplayed a major deal.
U.S. team of Mnuchin, Lighthizer, Ross, Navarro, Kudlow arriving for 3 May talks; ZTE case reinforces the tech fight; China still thought to believe more U.S. purchases can settle it.
Seven-year ZTE ban potentially devastating; U.S. firms supply 25–30% of ZTE components; China warned it will protect Chinese firms.
Neither side's $50B tariffs in effect yet; China targeted soy/aircraft to pressure farm-belt politics; ASA: devastating for every U.S. soybean farmer.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Engage the incoming U.S. delegation (Liu He–Mnuchin channel) without new structural commitments and without implementing additional tariffs beyond the lists already announced. Keep the April 4 $50 billion counter-list as leverage, put the ZTE denial order on the table as a condition for any cooling-off, and refuse to bargain away Made in China 2025 under a unilateral Section 301 frame. Do not offer a large purchase package as the deal itself until Washington has a matching offer to pause or narrow the 301 list.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not yet existential. The U.S. has moved from investigation to a proposed ~$50B/1,300-line Section 301 list aimed at aerospace, ICT, robotics and machinery — i.e., the industrial-upgrade sectors — and on 16 April activated a seven-year ZTE component ban that ZTE itself said threatens the firm’s survival. That combination sits toward the CHN +0.5 anchor (firm-level tech targeting plus a hit to export-tech ambitions) but stops short of +0.5–+1.0 because the 301 duties are still in comment period, not in force, and the real economy is not yet biting: industrial production is still ~6.8% YoY, merchandise exports are still expanding, CPI is soft, the discount rate is unchanged at 2.9%, reserves remain ~$3.13T, and CNY is around 6.36 after earlier appreciation — no FX or reserve crisis. April official manufacturing PMI eased and export orders slipped only to 50.7, still in expansion. Action should therefore be talks, not a new escalation. China already answered 232 with ~$3B (2 April) and answered the 301 list in kind with a proposed 25% on ~$50B including soybeans, autos and aircraft (4 April); a further hike on the eve of talks would likely harden Lighthizer/Navarro and bring forward U.S. implementation, while premature purchase concessions would validate unilateral 301 without removing ZTE or the tech list. MOFCOM has already said China will not negotiate under the 301 framework; the 2 May reporting is that a breakthrough on industrial policy is unlikely and Beijing will not accept preconditions on MIC 2025. The correct stance is therefore negotiate at 0: explore a pause, keep proportionate retaliation ready if Washington implements, and treat ZTE relief as the near-term test of whether talks are serious.
key_factors: ZTE seven-year U.S. component denial (16 Apr) is an immediate national-champion shock
Proposed $50B Section 301 list targets MIC 2025 sectors but is not yet in force
China already mirrored with $3B (232) and a proposed $50B (soy/autos/aircraft)
Liu He–Mnuchin talks opening with low expectations and a no-MIC-2025-preconditions line
Domestic macro still solid: IP ~6.8% YoY, exports up, reserves ~$3.13T, CNY stable, no financial-stress signal
Further escalation now risks locking in U.S. 301 implementation and a possible $100B add-on

sources_cited.excerpt: US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
USTR publishes proposed Section 301 tariff list: ~1,300 Chinese product lines (~$50B), targeting aerospace, ICT, robotics, machinery and related sectors.
China announces proposed retaliatory tariffs on ~$50B of US goods (including soybeans, automobiles, and aircraft) in response to the Section 301 list.
China imposes retaliatory tariffs on about $3B of US goods (pork, fruit, nuts, wine, and related items) in response to Section 232 steel/aluminum tariffs.

USTR releases Section 301 report finding China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable or discriminatory. Trump signs presidential memorandum directing tariffs on Chinese imports, a WTO case, and investment restrictions.
China industrial production latest 106.8 (2018-05-01), still expanding ~6.8% YoY; change +0.6 over the window.
China total reserves ex-gold latest ~$3.129T (2018-05-01), only about -0.95% over the window — no reserve-run signal.
CNY/USD 6.361 on 2018-05-02 after earlier appreciation from ~6.63; modest late-April softening, not a disorderly move.
China merchandise exports still expanding (latest ~$208.4B SA); +2.2% over the window — tariffs have not yet hit the export machine.

Most likely outcome of talks launching Thursday is an agreement to keep talking; breakthrough on China's economic policies highly unlikely; Chinese official: Beijing will not negotiate core interests nor accept preconditions including Made in China 2025.
BIS activated a denial of export privileges against ZTE after alleged false statements; Commerce framed it as regulatory enforcement, but it cuts ZTE off from U.S.-origin parts.
ZTE: the Denial Order will not only severely impact the survival and development of ZTE, but will also cause damages to all partners of ZTE including a large number of U.S. companies.
MOFCOM: we will not negotiate under the Section 301 framework. This is a basic principle, because the U.S. action is a unilateral one.
Chinese government will equivalently impose additional 25 percent tariff on U.S. products including soybean, automobiles, chemicals, airplanes.
April official manufacturing PMI eased; export-orders sub-index fell to 50.7 from 51.3 — early softness, still above 50.
